INTRODUCTION
 The Department of Health & Family Welfare
(DoHFW) is committed to ensure the highest
possible level of health and well-being of all
through a preventive and promotive healthcare
orientation in all developmental policies and

orientation in all developmental policies and
universal access to good quality health care services
while mitigating financial hardship. Towards this
objective, the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare
(MoHFW) is implementing various schemes,
programmes and national initiatives to provide
universal access to quality healthcare. The approach
is to increase access to decentralized public health
systems by establishing new infrastructure in
deficient areas and by upgrading the infrastructure

in existing institutions. There is also a need to
strengthen the role of the public sector in social
protection against the rising costs of healthcare
services and the need to provide a comprehensive
package of services with due prioritization to the
health of women and children.
 There has been a significant improvement in
creation of new facilities and infrastructure, and
e�orts are being made for adequate staffing of these
facilities by qualified health personnel. Availability

of drugs has improved at all levels and the robust
logistic arrangement for procurement and storage of
these drugs has been put in place.
 Ayushman Bharat, a flagship scheme of the
Government of India, was launched as
recommended by the National Health Policy 2017,
to achieve the vision of Universal Health Coverage
(UHC). This initiative has been designed to meet
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and its
underlying commitment, which is to "leave no one
behind".

behind".
 Ayushman Bharat is an attempt to move from
a sectoral and segmented approach of health service
delivery to a comprehensive need-based health care
service. This initiative aims to undertake path
breaking interventions to holistically address the
healthcare system (covering prevention, promotion
and ambulatory care) at primary, secondary and
tertiary level. It adopts a continuum of care
approach, comprising of four pillars, which are:
1) Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM)

1) Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM)
2) Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya
Yojana (AB PM-JAY)
3) Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)
4) Pradhan Mantri- Ayushman Bharat Health
Infrastructure Mission (PM- ABHIM)
 The existing Sub-Health Centres (SHCs) and
Primary Health Centres (PHCs) are being upgraded
to Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAMs) to deliver
universal, free comprehensive primary healthcare
services, with a focus on wellness and delivery of an

expanded range of services closer to the community.
The services span from promotive, preventive,
curative, rehabilitative and palliative care targeting
holistic healthcare service delivery. AAMs deliver
expanded range of services which go beyond
maternal and child healthcare services to include
care of non-communicable diseases, palliative and
rehabilitative care, oral, eye and ENT care, mental
health and first level for emergencies and trauma

health and first level for emergencies and trauma
management, including availability of free essential
drugs (106 drugs at SHCs, 172 at PHCs, 300 at
CHCs, 318 at SDHs and 381 drugs at DHs) and
diagnostic services (14 services at AAM-SHCs, 63
at PHCs, 97 at CHCs, 111 at SDHs and 134 at DHs)
at public health facilities.
 All AAM-PHCs and AAM-SHCs are
provided with sufficient space for outpatient care,
dispensing medicines, diagnostic services, adequate

spaces to display communication material of health
messages, including audio-visual aids and
appropriate community spaces for wellness
activities, including the practice of Yoga and
physical exercises.
 Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri-Jan
Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is a flagship scheme
of the Government which provides health cover of
Rs. 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and
tertiary care hospitalization to 12 crore families,
constituting the economically vulnerable bottom

constituting the economically vulnerable bottom
40% of India's population. On 29.10.2024, the
scheme was further extended to cover 6 Crore senior
citizens aged 70 years and above, representing 4.5

Crore families, through the Vay Vandana Card,
irrespective of their socio-economic status.
Additionally, AB PM-JAY now covers ASHA
workers, Anganwadi workers and their families,
providing Rs.5 lakh annual health cover, expanding
on previous social security benefits like free

on previous social security benefits like free
insurance premiums. This inclusion brings about 37
lakh ASHA families under the scheme for cashless,
quality secondary/ tertiary care.
 Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission
(ABDM) aims to create an online platform enabling
interoperability of health data within the health
ecosystem. Its core components include Ayushman
Bharat Health Account (ABHA) for citizens, Health
Professional Registry (HPR), Health Facility

Professional Registry (HPR), Health Facility
Registry (HFR) and ABHA Application. The digital
health ecosystem created by ABDM supports
continuity of care across primary, secondary and
tertiary healthcare in a seamless manner.
 Launched in 2021, Pradhan Mantri-
Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure
Mission (PM-ABHIM) is a Centrally Sponsored
Scheme with certain Central Sector components,
aimed at strengthening primary, secondary and
tertiary healthcare facilities. It focuses on enhancing

grassroots public health institutions to ensure
universal access to comprehensive primary
healthcare services, including diagnostics and
critical care. It emphasizes expansion of IT- enabled
disease surveillance systems to e�ectively detect,
investigate, prevent and manage public health
emergencies and disease outbreaks, making the
healthcare system more responsive during crisis.
Under PM-ABHIM, support is provided for
development of infrastructure, including Building-

less Sub-Centres in rural and urban areas, Block-
level Public Health Units, Integrated Public Health
Laboratories and Critical Care Hospital Blocks. As a
measure to strengthen emergency coordination and
on-site emergency care to disaster victims for better
disaster preparedness, fifty (50) Bharat Health
Initiative for Sahyog, Hita & Maitri (BHISHM)
Cubes have been deployed to AIIMS and other
Institutes of National Importance. These rapidly
deployable, Make in India cubes are modular units

deployable, Make in India cubes are modular units
that provide flexible emergency healthcare
infrastructure during disaster situations and mass
gatherings.

progress towards the commitments of National
Health Policy, 2017. The National Health Mission
(NHM), which is the flagship health systems reform
programme, provides a robust platform for
implementation of a range of interventions focused
on primary and secondary healthcare in rural and

on primary and secondary healthcare in rural and
urban areas. NHM's e�orts at strengthening health
systems in the States/UTs by allocating additional
financial resources, flexibility in design and
implementation ensured sharper focus on
particularly marginalized and vulnerable
populations and enabled us to achieve impressive
improvements in several key indicators of
Reproductive, Maternal, New-born, Child and
Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCHA+N)
and communicable diseases. NHM seeks to

 Guided by the National Health Policy 2017,
MoHFW has strengthened the public health
delivery system to ensure accessible, a�ordable and
quality healthcare. A cornerstone achievement is
operationalization of over 1.82 lakh AAMs as on
31.12.2025, aiming at providing Comprehensive
Primary Health Care. Leveraging technology to
bridge the rural-urban divide, e-Sanjeevani

bridge the rural-urban divide, e-Sanjeevani

 As per latest SRS (2021-23), the Maternal
Mortality Ratio (MMR) of India is 88 per lakh
live births against Sustainable Development Goal
(SDG) target of below 70 per lakh live births. Eight
States have achieved the SDG target of MMR viz.
Kerala (30), Maharashtra (36), Tamil Nadu (35),
Andhra Pradesh (30), Telangana (59), Jharkhand
(54), Gujarat (51) and Karnataka (68). MMR of

(54), Gujarat (51) and Karnataka (68). MMR of
India has reduced by 86% since 1990, far exceeding
the global average of 48%, as per current United
Nations Maternal Mortality Estimation Inter-
Agency Group (UN- MMEIG) Report 2000-2023.
 India has implemented a comprehensive
range of maternal health initiatives to ensure free
and equitable access to quality healthcare services
for all pregnant women and lactating mothers.
These initiatives include, Janani Suraksha Yojana

These initiatives include, Janani Suraksha Yojana
(JSY) which safe motherhood intervention by
encouraging institutional deliveries through
financial incentives and Janani Shishu Suraksha
Karyakram (JSSK) which provides free and
comprehensive care for pregnant women and
newborns in public health facilities.

 The Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva
Abhiyan (PMSMA) and Extended PMSMA
ensure quality antenatal check-ups and tracking of

the High-Risk Pregnancy (HRP), whereas the
Scheme for Optimizing Postnatal Care focuses on
early detection and timely management of post-
partum complications. The assured and respectful
service delivery initiatives like Surakshit Matritva
Aashwasan (SUMAN) is also being implemented.
 The Government is rolling out Midwifery
Services, functionalizing First Referral Units
(FRUs), establishing Maternal and Child Health
(MCH) Wings, Birth Waiting Homes (BWH) and

(MCH) Wings, Birth Waiting Homes (BWH) and
operationalizing obstetric High Dependency Units
(HDU) and Intensive Care Units (ICU). Together,
these initiatives and services ensure well-being of
mothers and their babies throughout pregnancy and
beyond.
 MoHFW launched the Nationwide campaign
"Swasth Nari, Sashakt Parivar Abhiyaan"
(SNSPA) from 17.09.2025 to 02.10.2025, focusing
on the health and nutrition of women, adolescent
girls and children, aiming to strengthen early

girls and children, aiming to strengthen early
detection, access to essential health services and
empower families to adopt healthier lifestyles for a
stronger and healthier India. The campaign was
inaugurated by the Hon'ble Prime Minister during
the national launch event held on 17.09.2025 at
Dhar, Madhya Pradesh. The campaign was
organized at all Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
(AAMs), Community Health Centers (CHCs) and
District Hospitals (DHs) across the country. The

District Hospitals (DHs) across the country. The
initiative also involved Central government
institutes, medical colleges and private
organizations. During the campaign, over 19 lakh
health camps were organized, registering a massive
footfall of nearly 11 Crore citizens nationwide.
 The Child Health programme under
RMNCHA+N strategy of NHM comprehensively
integrates the interventions which improve child
health and nutrition status, and addresses the factors

contributing to neonatal, infant, Under-Five
mortality and malnutrition.
 According to the latest Sample Registration
System (SRS) Report 2023, India's Under-Five
Mortality Rate is 29 per 1,000 live births, the Infant
Mortality Rate is 25 per 1,000 live births, and the
Neonatal Mortality rate is 19 per 1,000 live births.
As per the report, eight (8) States/ UTs have already
achieved the SDG target for neonatal mortality
(NMR ≤12 by 2030) [i.e. Kerala (4), Delhi (9), Tamil

Nadu (9), Jammu & Kashmir (10), Maharashtra
(11), Himachal Pradesh (11), Karnataka (11) and
Punjab (12)] also thirteen (13) States/ UTs have
also met the SDG target for Under-five mortality
(U5MR ≤25 by 2030) i.e. [Kerala (8), Tamil Nadu
(13), Jammu & Kashmir (15), Delhi (16),
Maharashtra (16), Himachal Pradesh (17),
Karnataka (17), West Bengal (18), Andhra Pradesh
(21), Punjab (22), Telangana (22), Gujarat (23) and
Uttarakhand (23)].
 As per the UN Inter-Agency Group for Child

As per the UN Inter-Agency Group for Child
Mortality Estimation (UN IGME) Report released
on 25.03.2025, India achieved a 78% decline in the
Under-Five Mortality Rate (U5MR) surpassing the
global reduction of 61% and 70% decline in the
Neonatal Mortality Rate (NMR) compared to 54%
globally in during 1990-2023. UNIGME identifies
India as an exemplar for its demonstrable success in
reducing child mortality through effective strategies
and policies.
 Various facility-based and community-

Various facility-based and community-
based interventions are also being implemented to
reduce child morbidity and mortality. As of now,
1,114 Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs)/
Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) have been
established at District Hospitals and Medical
Colleges to provide round- the-clock care for sick
newborns. Additionally, 3,215 Newborn
Stabilization Units (NBSUs) at FRUs and CHCs
level, along with 22,150 Newborn Care Corners

level, along with 22,150 Newborn Care Corners
(NBCCs) at delivery points, have been sanctioned to
ensure availability of essential and emergency
newborn care. Recently, MoHFW released revised
Operational Guidelines on Facility-Based Newborn
Care (FBNC) and training modules on Oxygen
Support System for Newborns and Empowering
Mothers and Caregivers in providing Nurturing
Care to small and sick newborns. These revised
FBNC guidelines and training modules strengthen

FBNC guidelines and training modules strengthen
the quality of care for small and sick newborns by
improving clinical practices, ensuring safer oxygen
management and empowering families to support
optimal newborn growth and development.
 MoHFW has released operational guidelines
on Stillbirth Surveillance and Response in Public
Health Facilities. These initiatives are critical
towards achieving Sustainable Development Goal

 Under community-based initiatives, Home
Based Newborn Care (HBNC) and Home-Based
Care for Young Child (HBYC) programmes are
implemented through scheduled home visits by
ASHAs in the country. These visits empower
families as well as facilitate early identification of
danger signs and timely referral to health facilities.
ASHAs act as a crucial bridge between the

ASHAs act as a crucial bridge between the
community and health facilities, with the aim of
reducing child morbidity and mortality. During FY
2024-25, around 1.51 Crore newborns were visited,
and more than 73 lakh newborns were visited upto
Quarter 2 (April–September) of FY 2025-26.
Similarly, a total of 4.81 Crore home visits were
conducted for young children (3-15 months) in FY
2024-25, and 2.98 Crore visits were conducted by
Quarter 2 (April- September) of FY 2025-26. The

Quarter 2 (April- September) of FY 2025-26. The
programmatic intervention focuses strongly on "at-
risk" children at the community level.
 Under Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram
(RBSK), the focus is on early identification of 4D's
and management of health conditions. 11,472
Mobile Health Teams screen children in the age
group of 0-18 years of age at Anganwadi Centres
and Schools. 451 District Early Intervention
Centres (DEICs) have been set up for therapeutic

Centres (DEICs) have been set up for therapeutic
management and follow-up care. These
interventions aim to enhance the overall quality of
life of children through early detection and
intervention for birth defects, diseases, deficiencies,
and developmental delays (4Ds), while also helping
to reduce out-of-pocket expenditure for families.
During April-June, 2025 (Q1 of FY 2025-26), 4.72
Crore children were screened; 33.32 lakh children
were identified with any of 4Ds; 24.31 lakh children

availed services in secondary tertiary facilities.
 MoHFW is implementing several integrated
nutrition specific programmes in life cycle approach
for interrupting the inter-generational cycle of
under-nutrition, such as Nutrition Rehabilitation

Implementation of SNA, the States are required to

within a period of 21 & 40 days respectively.

1.2.1 INTRODUCTION
The National Health Mission (NHM) is a
comprehensive initiative designed to provide
universal access to equitable, affordable, and high-
quality healthcare that remains responsive to the
needs of all citizens. National Rural Health
Mission (NRHM) was launched on 12.04.2005, to
specifically target the healthcare needs of rural and
vulnerable populations. On 01.05.2013, the Mission
was expanded to include the National Urban

was expanded to include the National Urban
Health Mission (NUHM) as a Sub-Mission,
establishing the overarching NHM framework. The
Mission focuses on strengthening health systems,
managing Reproductive-Maternal-Neonatal-Child
and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A), and
controlling both communicable and non-
communicable diseases.
Further, the Union Cabinet, vide its decision dated
21.03.2018, approved continuation of National
Health Mission (NHM) from 01.04.2017 to

Health Mission (NHM) from 01.04.2017 to
31.03.2020. Department of Expenditure, vide O.M.
dated 10.01.2020, accorded approval for interim
extension of NHM for a period till 31.03.2021 or till
the date the recommendations of 15th Finance
Commission come into effect, whichever is earlier.
Further, the Government of India accorded the
approval for continuation of NHM from 01.04.2021
to 31.03.2026 or till further review as
communicated vide Department of Expenditure's

communicated vide Department of Expenditure's
O.M. No. 01(01)/PFC-1/2022 dated 01.02.2022.

1.2.4 IMPROVEMENT IN THE QUALITY
OF HEALTHCARE
The status of health care of a country is reflected
through the pattern of basic demographic indicators.
The huge success of the Health and Family Welfare
programmes in India is clearly evident from the
trend of such indicators since independence and in
particular since the new millennium based on the

particular since the new millennium based on the
estimates from the Sample Registration System
(SRS) of Registrar General & Census
Commissioner, India (RGI), M/o Home Affairs as
given in Table 1. The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) of the
country has more than halved from 40.8 births per
1000 population in 1951 to 18.4 births in 2023.
Similarly, the Crude Death Rate (CDR) has also
experienced a fall from 25.1 deaths per 1000
population in 1951 to 8.4 in 2001 and further to 6.4

deaths in 2023 indicating India has prevented
around 18.7 deaths per 1000 population since 1951.
India has witnessed a significant demographic
transition, marked by a substantial decline in the
Total Fertility Rate (TFR) from 6.0 children per
woman in 1951 to 3.1 in 2001, and further to 1.9 in
2023. This decline reflects sustained efforts in
population stabilization, improved access to
healthcare, and rising awareness around
reproductive choices. In recent years, India has also

witnessed a notable improvement in maternal health
by bringing down the Maternal Mortality Ratio to
88 maternal deaths per 100000 live births in 2021-
23, from 301 during (2001-03).
Similarly, India has also experienced notable
improvement in child mortality by reducing the
Neo-natal Mortality Rate (NNMR) from 40 deaths
per 1000 live births during 2001 to 19 in 2023 and
Under Five Mortality Rate (Per 1000 live births) by
reducing from 59 in 2010 to 29 in 2023. During the

last two decades, India has added more than five
years to average life expectancy at birth of its
population from 63.4 years in 1999-2003 (mid-year
2001) to 70.3 years in 2019-23 (mid-year 2022).

Introduction
Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya
Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is the world's largest publicly
funded health assurance scheme, launched on
September 23, 2018, with the vision of achieving
Universal Health Coverage (UHC) as envisaged
under Sustainable Development Goal 3.8. The
scheme aims to provide financial protection against
catastrophic health expenditure and ensure access to
quality healthcare for India's economically
vulnerable population.

vulnerable population.
AB PM-JAY provides a health cover of Rs.5 lakh
per family per year for secondary and tertiary care
hospitalization to over 12 crore poor and vulnerable
families i.e. nearly 40% of India's population. The
scheme is entirely cashless and paperless, delivered
through empanelled public and private health care
providers, ensuring that beneficiaries can avail
treatment without financial hardship at the point of
service delivery.

1.7.1 THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR
VECTOR BORNE DISEASES CONTROL
(NCVBDC)
The National Center for Vector Borne Diseases
Control (NCVBDC) is an umbrella programme for
prevention and control of vector borne diseases viz.
Malaria, Japanese Encephalitis (JE), Dengue,
Chikungunya, Kala-azar and Lymphatic Filariasis.
Out of these six diseases, three diseases namely

Out of these six diseases, three diseases namely
Kala-azar, Lymphatic Filariasis and Malaria are
targeted for elimination according to SDG. The
States/UTs are responsible for implementation of
the programme, whereas NCVBDC provides
technical and financial assistance to the States/UTs
in the form of cash & commodity, under the
overarching umbrella scheme of NHM. Malaria,
Filaria, JE, Dengue and Chikungunya are
transmitted by mosquitoes whereas Kala-azar is

transmitted by mosquitoes whereas Kala-azar is
transmitted by sand-flies. The transmission of
vector borne diseases depends on prevalence of
infective vectors and human-vector contact, which
is further influenced by vector bionomics,
ecological and social factors like climatic change,
sleeping habits of human, type of vector, density and
biting habit of vectors, migration of human
population and developmental activities.
Strategies for prevention and control of Vector

Strategies for prevention and control of Vector
Borne Diseases (VBDs) under NCVBDC are as
follows:
1. Integrated Vector Management includes Indoor
Residual Spraying (IRS) in selected high-risk areas,
Long Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs) in high
malaria endemic areas, use of larvivorous fish, anti-
larval measures in urban areas including bio-
larvicides and minor environmental engineering
and source reduction for prevention of mosquito
breeding.
2. Disease Management involves early case

2. Disease Management involves early case
detection with active, passive and sentinel
surveillance followed by complete and effective
treatment, strengthening of referral services,
epidemic preparedness, and rapid response. Annual
Mass Drugs Administration (MDA) and Morbidity
Management and Disability Prevention (MMDP)
for Lymphatic Filariasis.
3. Supportive Interventions aim at Behavior
Change Communication (BCC), Inter- Sectoral
Convergence and Human Resource Development

Convergence and Human Resource Development
through capacity building.

Malaria is a parasitic disease caused by parasite
Plasmodium having five known species namely,
Plasmodium vivax (P. vivax), Plasmodium

Dengue & Chikungunya
Dengue and Chikungunya are a rapidly spreading,
outbreak-prone arboviral disease transmitted by
Aedes mosquitoes. Aedes aegypti is the primary
vector, while Aedes albopictus has also been

vector, while Aedes albopictus has also been
implicated in transmission in several States.
Currently, there is no specific drug or vaccine
available for Dengue and Chikungunya. Maximum
number of cases are reported during the monsoon
and post-monsoon seasons. Additionally, increases
in temperature also lead to paradigm shift of
transmission of both diseases from seasonal to
perennial in many parts of the Country especially in
southern and western States. Rising temperatures

southern and western States. Rising temperatures
accelerate the mosquito life cycle, shortening the
time it takes for eggs to develop into adults. Warmer
conditions reduce the extrinsic incubation period of
pathogens within mosquitoes. Higher temperatures
also enable mosquitoes to survive and thrive in
regions that were previously too cold, expanding
their geographical range.
In addition, climate change, unplanned
urbanization, population movement, developmental

urbanization, population movement, developmental
activities, changes in human behaviours, spreading

Japanese Encephalitis:
• Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is an arbo-viral disease
caused by JE virus.
• It is transmitted through the bite of infected Culex
vishnui group of mosquitoes, mainly by Culex
tritaeniorhyncus. These mosquitoes mostly breed
in the rice fields, irrigation cannels, puddles of
rural areas.
• JE occurs mainly during the monsoon season in the
month of July to September & also some cases

month of July to September & also some cases
occur in the post monsoon season (October and
November).
• JE is reported under Acute Encephalitis Syndrome
(AES), which may be caused, by a wide variety of
viruses, bacteria, protozoa, etc.
• JE presents in the severe form as the virus infects
the brain causing encephalitis, which is
manifested by rapid onset of high fever, headache,
neck stiffness, disorientation, coma, seizures,
spastic paralysis (hemiplegia, paraplegia etc.) and
ultimately death.

ultimately death.
• Now days, 10–15% patient who survive have
permanent neurologic or psychiatric sequelae
which may include permanent behavioural or
neurological problems such as paralysis, recurrent
seizures or the inability to speak and listen.
• There is no cure for the disease. Treatment is
symptomatic and is focused on relieving clinical
signs and symptoms.
• JE is the only vector borne disease where safe and
effective vaccines are available to prevent JE

with weak immune systems, including young
children and those living with HIV. It also affects
people with specific conditions like malnutrition,
diabetes mellitus (DM), silicosis and existing
disabilities, as well as those who smoke or have
substance-use disorders.

b) Screen 100% among those attending special

TRANSPLANTATION OF HUMAN ORGANS
AND TISSUES ACT, 1994. AND RELATED
LEGAL FRAMEWORK
Organ donation and transplantation is a
Government regulated activity in India as per
the provisions of the Transplantation of Human
Organs and Tissues Act 1994 (as amended in 2011).
This legislation aims to regulate the removal,
storage, and transplantation of human organs for
therapeutic purposes while strictly prohibiting any
commercial dealing in organs and tissues. The

commercial dealing in organs and tissues. The
Amendmed Act has been adopted by all States/UTs
except State of Andhra Pradesh.
Brain Stem death is recognized as legal death in
India under the aforesaid Act, like many other
countries, which has revolutionized the concept of
organ donation after death. After natural/cardiac
death usually only a few tissues can be donated (like
cornea, bone, skin etc.), whereas after brain stem
death up to 8 lifesaving organs such as kidneys,

death up to 8 lifesaving organs such as kidneys,
heart, liver, lungs, Pancreas and Intestine and in
addition many types of tissues like cornea, skin,
heart valves, bones etc. can be donated.
The Government of India has notified in the Gazette
- Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues
Rules (amendment), 2025 - amending Form-15
under the Transplantation of Human Organs and
Tissues Rules, 2014, published on 6th November,
2025, whereby the requirement of a clinical

2025, whereby the requirement of a clinical
specular microscope for registration of corneal
transplantation centres has been made optional. The
amendment is expected to help address the large
unmet need for corneas in the country and improve
access to corneal transplantation services,
particularly in rural and semiurban areas, by
facilitating registration of smaller hospitals and
centres. Since transplant centres are authorised to
harvest corneas from deceased donors, this step is

expected to enhance both donation and
transplantation rates in the country.
National Organ Transplant Program –
Objective and Implementation
The Government of India is implementing the
National Organ Transplant Program (NOTP), a
central sector scheme to enhance access to life-
saving transplantations, improve awareness about
healthy lifestyle, prevention of organ failure and
deceased organs and tissues donation, augmenting
infrastructure for organ donation, transplantation

and tissue banking especially in Government
institutions, and capacity building of manpower and
research.
In pursuance to the mandate given under
Transplantation of Human Organs & Tissues Act
1994, Government of India has setup 3 tier structure
of Organ and Tissue Transplant Organizations, one
at the national level (NOTTO), and 5 at the regional
level (ROTTO) and 26 State levels (SOTTO),
which network with organ and tissue
transplant/retrieval hospitals/centres and tissue

transplant/retrieval hospitals/centres and tissue
banks to provide for an efficient and organized
system of organ procurement and distribution in the
country and to maintain a national registry of donors
and recipients of human organs and tissues.
The network at present is linked with 1090
Hospitals including 764 transplant centres, 149 Non
Transplant Organ Retrieval Centres (NTORCs) and
177 Tissue Banks (Biomaterial Centres).

An enduring vision, an indomitable spirit and an

of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences (NIMHANS).
From the lunatic asylum in the nineteenth century to
the Mysore Government Mental Hospital in 1936,

status of Institute of National Importance (INI)

Spread over an area of nearly 135 acres, NIMHANS
combines mental health and neurosciences under
one roof. Such a unique approach has made
NIMHANS a premier institute of international
repute. Its priorities include service delivery,
training, research and policy formulation. Although

intended as a tertiary care referral centre for mental,
neurological and neurosurgical disorders, its
reputation as a centre of excellence for clinical care
attracts people from all parts of India as well as other
countries. The therapeutic modalities blend the
modern systems of medicine with traditional
systems of care and management.
NIMHANS is the leading post-graduate training
centre in the country in mental health and
neurosciences. Occupying a pre-eminent position, it

currently offers over 100 courses including MCh,
DM, MD, post-doctoral fellowships, doctoral
studies, MPhil, MSc, diplomas and more recently,
undergraduate courses in select disciplines.
NIMHANS has emerged as a leader in both
behavioural and neurosciences research. At
NIMHANS, research occurs in a seamless manner
from the bench to the bedside and from the bedside
to the community. The institute has made signal
contributions in a multitude of areas: from addiction

to Alzheimer's; from imaging to intensive care;
from brain injury to interventional neuroradiology;
from disaster relief to deep brain stimulation; from
stroke research to signalling in the brain; from
rabies to retroviral infections; from youth mental
health to yoga research; from molecular genetics to
mindfulness research; from restoration to
rehabilitation.
NIMHANS plays a pivotal role in national policy
and programming and is in the forefront of setting

the agenda for mental health in India. The flagship
District Mental Health Programme of the
Government of India emerged out of the Bellary
model of care, piloted by NIMHANS. The Institute
continues to provide the impetus to strategize,
strengthen and bring in innovation in both
institutional and community-based mental health
care services across the country. We have

Sciences (AIIMS); and

Colleges/Institutions in a phased manner.

quality medical education and nursing education
along with tertiary health care facilities to the

Promoting quality research and innovation in bio-
medical field is a key focus area of new AIIMS.

number of research papers published by these
AIIMS. During FY 2024-25, total 3473 research

research journals. There is increased use of digital
interventions for promoting quality outcomes in the
research field. Indian Council of Medical Research

(ICMR) and Department of Science & Technology
(DST) have been providing research grants for
taking up research projects in new AIIMS.
Important focus areas in medical and bio-medical
research include robot-assisted surgery, AI-based
diagnosis, use of AI technology in medical imaging
& digital pathology, drug discovery, genomics and
personalised medicine. Innovations like tele-
medicine and use of drones for sample collection in
remote areas are being promoted. Student exchange

remote areas are being promoted. Student exchange
programme amongst the AIIMS has also been taken
up as a measure to facilitate sharing of best practices
and giving better exposure to the medical students in
new AIIMS.

3. Research Accomplishments
The Institute promotes communication and
disorders research by emphasising clinically
relevant applied research on causes, control and
prevention of communication disorders, assessment
and treatment issues, and the testing and refinement

of new technologies for speech and hearing
impairment. Six funded research projects were
completed, 72 and were progressing in different
departments of the Institute. The Govt. of India
funding agencies like the Department of Science
and Technology sponsored the projects in addition
to the grant given by the Institute. In total, 125
scientific papers were published in various peer-

international and national scientific conferences

international and national scientific conferences

1. Introduction:
The Central Leprosy Teaching and Research
Institute (CLT&RI), is the apex and one among four
leprosy institutes established under Directorate
General of Health Services (DGHS), and situated at
Chengalpattu, Tamil Nadu. The institution was
constituted in the year 1955 under a Governing
Body by taking over the Lady Wellington Leprosy
Sanatorium set up in 1924, and was subsequently

Sanatorium set up in 1924, and was subsequently
made a Subordinate Office of the DGHS in 1974.
The key objectives of the institute are to provide
diagnostic, treatment and referral services to
Persons affected with leprosy (PAL), train
manpower for National Leprosy Eradication
Programme (NLEP), Monitoring & Evaluation of
NLEP, and to conduct basic and operational
research. The Institute has a 124 bed hospital
catering to both indoor and outdoor patients with

catering to both indoor and outdoor patients with
four technical divisions: - Clinical, Surgical,
Laboratory and Epidemiology & Statistics.

1. Integrated Disease Surveillance
Programme (IDSP)
Integrated Disease Surveillance Program is a
disease surveillance program under National Health
Mission that does the disease surveillance in the
country. It was initiated in 2004, with the objective-

• to strengthen and maintain decentralized
laboratory-based IT enabled disease
surveillance system for epidemic prone
diseases
• to monitor disease trends
• to detect and respond to outbreaks in the early
rising phase
• creation of trained cadre of Rapid Response
Team (RRTs) at the District, State & National
levels
Under this program there is a Central surveillance
Unit (CSU) at Central level, State Surveillance Unit
(SSU) at the State/UTs level and District

(SSU) at the State/UTs level and District
Surveillance Unit (DSU) at district level. The
program is responsible for the surveillance of 50
plus epidemic prone diseases.
In the year 2021, the programme has shifted from a

in the country's healthcare information delivery

4.1 INTRODUCTION
The Central Government has set up regulatory
bodies for monitoring the standard of medical,
Dental and nursing education, promoting training
and research activities. This is being done with a
view to sustain the production of medical and allied

health care manpower to meet the requirement of
health care delivery system at the primary,
secondary and tertiary levels in country.
4.2 NATIONAL MEDICAL COMMISSION
(NMC)
1.1 The National Medical Commission Act, 2019,
for setting up a National Medical Commission
(NMC) and to repeal the Indian Medical Council
Act 1956 received assent of the President on
08.08.2019. The NMC was constituted with effect
from 25.09.2020.
The Act provides for constitution of four

The Act provides for constitution of four
Autonomous Boards namely Under Graduate
Medical Education Board (UGMEB), Post
Graduate Medical Board (PGMEB), Medical
Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) and Ethics
and Medical Registration Board (EMRB).
1.2 This is a historic reform aimed to steer the
direction of medical education towards a
transparent, qualitative and accountable system.
The basic premise and principle change that has
occured is that the Regulator is now selected on

occured is that the Regulator is now selected on
merit, as opposed to an elected regulator.
Professionals with impeccable integrity, vast
experience, and high stature have been now placed
at the helm to steer the medical education reforms
further. Constitution of NMC paves the way for
continuation and deepening of reforms. To promote
affordability, the Act empowers the Commission to
frame guidelines for determining fees and other
charges for 50% of seats in private medical colleges

and deemed universities. This Act also provides for
the rating of medical colleges, helping students
make well-informed choices. Additionally, the
Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) of
MEDICAL, DENTAL, NURSING
& ALLIED HEALTH EDUCATION
the NMC maintains an electronic National Medical
Register (NMR), which records the name, address,
and all recognized qualifications of licensed
medical practitioners. The NMR is a
comprehensive and regularly updated database of

comprehensive and regularly updated database of
all allopathic (MBBS) registered doctors in India. A
key feature of the NMR is its linkage with doctors'
Aadhaar IDs, which ensures the authenticity of each
practitioner.
1.3 The National Medical Commission has
notified Medical Institutions (Qualifications of
Faculty) Regulations, 2025 to address the shortage
of qualified teaching faculty. The regulations
broaden eligibility by permitting non-medical
M.Sc. and Ph.D. holders as faculty in relevant

M.Sc. and Ph.D. holders as faculty in relevant
specialties, recognizing certain clinical and super-
specialty experiences as valid teaching experience,
and allowing transitional faculty appointments
where specialists are unavailable. They also enable
overseas-qualified Indian MBBS graduates from
select English-speaking countries to serve as
Assistant Professors or Senior Residents, permit
experienced non-teaching consultants and
government hospital specialists to join as Assistant

Professors with prescribed conditions, and allow
diploma holders with sufficient cumulative
experience to be appointed to faculty positions,
thereby strengthening faculty availability in
medical institutions.

PROGRAMME, MoHFW
As per the provision made under the Constitution of
India, under Article 47, the Cabinet Sub-Committee

has recommended to set up National 'Drug De-
addiction Programme (DDAP)' which came into
force in 1988. The objectives of the Programme is to
provide affordable, easily accessible and evidence-
based treatment for all substance use disorders
through the government health care facilities and to
build the capacities of health care staff in
recognition and management of substance use
disorders.
The programme is being implemented through six
health institutes of Ministry of Health & Family

health institutes of Ministry of Health & Family
Welfare namely National Drug Dependence
Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS, New Delhi;
PGIMER, Chandigarh; NIMHANS, Bengaluru;
Dr.RML Hospital, New Delhi; AIIMS,
Bhubaneswar; and CIP, Ranchi. Out of these six
institutes, the centre running at NDDTC, AIIMS,
New Delhi is functioning as the National Nodal
centre and coordinating with other major
component of the DDAP of the "DTC Scheme".
Under this Programme 25 Drug Treatment Clinics

Under this Programme 25 Drug Treatment Clinics
are functional in District level Civil Hospitals or in
Medical Colleges across the country, which
provides OPD Services to the drug addicted
patients. Ministry of Health & Family Welfare
provides funds to these six institutes for
implementing the Programme.
The details of achievement made by the six DDAP
institutes are given below:
I. National Drug Dependence Treatment
Centre, AIIMS, New Delhi.
The National Drug Treatment Centre, Ghaziabad

The National Drug Treatment Centre, Ghaziabad
(NDDTC), AIIMS has been established as the apex
Centre for treatment of drugs and substance use
disorders. This Centre is working in
multidimensional area of drugs and it has a well-
equipped laboratory to detect various drugs in body
fluids and for biochemical investigations.
a) Clinical Statistics
During the period Jan- September 2025, the Centre
registered 4757 new patients and provide follow up
treatment of 2,33,585 patients. The Centre had

treatment of 2,33,585 patients. The Centre had
provided in-patient care to 862 patients from their 50
beded ward during the specified period. NDDTC
laboratory conducted 65986 biochemistry, 52630
haematology, 683 HIV Screening and 86027 Urine
drug screening test during the said period in its
toxicology, hematology, biochemistry and HIV
screening labs. HIV screening is essential for
individuals with drug addiction because their
behaviors place them at a significantly higher risk of

HIV acquisition and transmission like sharing
needles, syringes or other equipment to inject drugs.
Early diagnosis through screening allows for timely
treatment, which improves health outcomes and
drastically reduces the spread of the virus to others.
NDDTC, AIIMS also facilitate to run 25 Drug

International health is becoming a major concern
due to spread of various infectious diseases
affecting global health security, that can be achieved

by developing a robust surveillance and response
system through exemplary public health approach.
The Points of Entry (POEs) serve as India's first line
of defence against Public Health threat's, including
Chemical, Biological, and Radio-nuclear (CBRN)
hazards. They play a crucial role in preventing the
transmission of diseases through passengers,
conveyances, and cargo across borders and ensuring
a safe environment. These entry points are
strategically positioned to monitor, assess and

strategically positioned to monitor, assess and
respond to health risks associated with international
travel and trade.
In India, the responsibility for securing public
health at PoEs rests with competent health
establishments known as Airport Health
Organizations (APHOs), Port Health Organizations
(PHOs), and Land Port Health Organizations
(LPHOs). These establishments are subordinate
offices of Public Health (International Health)
Division, Directorate General of Health Services,

Division, Directorate General of Health Services,
each tailored to address the unique challenges and
health risks associated with international travel and
trade at their respective points of entry.
Additionally, these health units also ensure
compliance with International Health Regulations
(2005), Indian Aircraft (Public Health) Rules
(1954), and The Indian Port Health Rules (1955).

critical functions, including International health

ELIMINATION PROGRAMME
Strengthening TB Care among Tribal
Populations
The National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme
(NTEP) has prioritized tribal populations as a key

vulnerable group since 2005 through dedicated
Tribal Action Plans. The Programme ensures
equitable access to TB care services for all,
irrespective of caste, gender, or religion.
Recognizing the distinct challenges faced by tribal,
hilly, and hard-to-reach populations, NTEP has
introduced special provisions to improve access and
service coverage, including:
• TB Programme Management Unit (TB Unit)
which is 1 TB Unit for every 1 lakh population
in tribal, hilly and difficult area as against 1

in tribal, hilly and difficult area as against 1
TB Unit for every 2 lakhs general population.
Every TB Unit is supported with a programme
supervisory staff for management of
diagnosis and treatment services in the area.
• Support for transportation of patient and
attendant in tribal areas – Patients from tribal /
hilly/difficult areas are being provided an
aggregate amount of Rs. 750 to cover travel
costs of patient and attendant.
Despite these efforts, geographical isolation,

Despite these efforts, geographical isolation,
nutritional vulnerabilities, cultural barriers, and
health-system gaps continue to constrain access and
utilization of TB services among tribal
communities. To address these persistent
challenges, NTEP, in collaboration with the
Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA), launched the
Tribal TB Initiative in March 2021, aligning TB
elimination efforts with the broader tribal health and
social protection framework.

Malaria:
The malaria disease burden in India has declined by

78.15% (from 1.16 million to 0.25 million) and
malaria deaths by 77.6% (from 384 to 86) in 2024 as
compared to 2015. Malaria is more predominant in
tribal districts of North-Eastern States, Odisha,
Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand. Among 182 tribal and
Left-Wing Extremist (LWE) districts, there has
been 80.32% reduction in malaria morbidity and
79.12% reduction in malaria mortality in 2024 as
compared to 2015.
Under NVBDCP, various anti-malarial
interventions such as Early diagnosis and radical

interventions such as Early diagnosis and radical
treatment, Case-based surveillance and rapid
response, Integrated vector management (IVM),
Epidemic preparedness and early response,
Monitoring, Evaluation, Advocacy, Coordination,
Partnerships, Behaviour change communication
and community mobilization are undertaken. Along
with NHM, externally aided Global Fund project is
being implemented in high endemic States. A total
of 1.58 crores Long- lasting insecticidal nets

of 1.58 crores Long- lasting insecticidal nets
(LLINs) under GFTAM support were supplied to
the community residing in high malaria endemic
areas of 7 North Eastern States, Chhattisgarh, and
Madhya Pradesh in 2024.

Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri- Jan Arogya
Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is the world's largest health
assurance scheme that intends to minimise the out-
of-pocket expenditure of the target beneficiaries
arising due to catastrophic expenditure on
healthcare. The scheme provides health cover of Rs.
5 lakhs per family per year for secondary and

5 lakhs per family per year for secondary and
tertiary care hospitalization to over 55 crores poor
and vulnerable individuals corresponding to 12
crore families that form the bottom 40% of the
Indian population. The households included in the
scheme are based on the deprivation and
occupational criteria of Socio-Economic Caste
Census 2011 (SECC) and other State schemes that
consider similar deprivation criterion as of AB-
PMJAY. The scheme was launched subsuming the

PMJAY. The scheme was launched subsuming the
erstwhile Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana
(RSBY) on 23.09.2018 with an aim to improve
affordability, accessibility and quality of healthcare
for the poor and vulnerable section of the
population.
Salient Features of AB PM-JAY
• Around 12 Crore poor and vulnerable
families (approximately 55 crore
individuals) are entitled under AB PM-JAY
for cashless and paperless healthcare
services of upto 5 lakhs annually which can
be accessed at any of the AB-PMJAY

be accessed at any of the AB-PMJAY
empanelled hospitals.
• The beneficiaries can avail healthcare
services across 27 specialities covering
1949 procedures. This health cover
includes 3 days of pre-hospitalisation and
15 days of post-hospitalisation expenses.
• There is no cap on family size, age or gender
to ensure that all members of the beneficiary
families are covered.
The benefits under the scheme are portable across
the country.
• The scheme is implemented in convergence

with the State schemes where the State
governments have identified other
beneficiaries based on similar parameter as
of AB PM-JAY.

Introduction:
Iodine is an essential micronutrient required daily at
100-150 micrograms for normal human growth and
development. Deficiency of iodine can cause
physical and mental retardation, cretinism,
abortions, stillbirth, deaf mutism, squint & various
types of goitre. As per the surveys conducted by the
Directorate General of Health Services, Indian
Council of Medical Research, Health Institutions
and the State Health Directorates, it has been found

that out of 414 districts surveyed in all the 29 States
and 7 UTs, 337 districts are endemic i.e. where the
prevalence of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDDs)
is more than 5%.
Realizing the magnitude of the problem, the
Government of India launched a 100 per cent
centrally assisted National Goitre Control
Programme (NGCP) in 1962. In August, 1992 the
National Goitre Control Programme (NGCP) was
renamed as National Iodine Deficiency Disorders
Control Programme (NIDDCP) with a view of wide

Control Programme (NIDDCP) with a view of wide
spectrum of Iodine Deficiency Disorders like
mental and physical retardation, deaf mutism,
cretinism, still births, abortions etc.

Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic
Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act,
1994
With an objective to prohibit sex selection and
regulate the ethical medical use of Pre-Natal

regulate the ethical medical use of Pre-Natal
Diagnostic techniques, the Pre-natal Diagnostic
Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse)
Act, 1994 (PNDT Act), was brought into operation
from 01.01.1996. The PNDT Act has further been
amended to make it more comprehensive. The
amended Act came into force with effect from
14.02.2003 and was rechristened as “Pre-
conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques
(Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994”

(Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994”
(PC&PNDT Act) to make it more stringent. The
possibility of sex selection, before conception has
been brought within the ambit of this Act so as to
pre-empt the misuse of such diagnostic
technologies, which might contribute to decline in
Sex Ratio at Birth (SRB). Use of ultrasound/
imaging machines and all pre-conception diagnostic
techniques have been brought within the purview of
this Act, more explicitly, so as to curb their misuse

for detection and disclosure of sex of the foetus.
More stringent punishments are prescribed under
the Act, so as to serve as a deterrent against
violations of the Act. The implementation of the Act
has been entrusted with the States/UTs and District
Authorities, where the notified Appropriate
Authorities are empowered to search, seize and seal
the machines, equipment and records of the
violators of law including sealing of premises and
commissioning of witnesses under the PC&PNDT

Policy
In pursuance of the Official Language Policy of the
Government of India, all documents covered under
Section 3(3) of the Official Languages Act, 1963 are
being issued in both languages i.e. Hindi and
English. Action plan is prepared on the basis of
checkpoints identified in the Ministry to ensure
compliance with the Official Language Policy. The

an effective strategy for implementation of the

targets set in the Annual Programme issued by the

In order to encourage the use of Hindi in official

works and among the officers/ employees of the
Ministry, Hindi Fortnight was organized
successfully in the Ministry during 14-30
September, 2025. During the fortnight, eight
competitions namely, Quiz competition, Essay
competition, Hindi Noting and Drafting, Extempore
and poetry recitation as well as Hindi Dictation
Competition were organized. The winners of these
competitions were awarded cash prizes as well as
certificates.

under the chairmanship of the Union Home
Minister.
